title: Whole Ones Tray
description: Pour loose parts into whole ones until no more will fill, and read the two ways of writing what you hold.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

writeup.why: Gather loose parts into whole ones, and find the two different ways of writing what you are holding.
writeup.look: A tray of empty whole circles on the left, a heap of equal loose parts on the right, and both readings written under them at once.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Whole Ones Tray' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the parts poured against the parts the heap began with, two numbers in ink, and under them the part size written in words, sixths or eighths or sevenths, which is the number pinned across the top and is the one thing on this stage that does not change. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The tray fills the left of the working area, 560 by 396 at 64,202, drawn as up to nine empty whole circles of radius 84 in rows, each ruled into the pinned number of equal parts by near-black lines before anything is poured, so a whole one can be counted whether it is full or not. The heap waits at 660,202, 420 by 396, loose parts all of one size and one shape, separated and never overlapping, at most sixty of them. The part size is pinned at 64,150, 300 by 40, and cannot be edited while a conversion is running; a tap on it during one prints that the parts would have to be recut and changes nothing. Pour moves parts one at a time into the whole ones, filling each circle completely before starting the next, and the two readings run under the tray at 64,610 and 64,668, each 560 by 46 and neither ever hidden: the single fraction, counting every part over the pinned size, and the mixed number, counting the filled wholes and then the parts still loose. The sorter is 420 by 76 at 660,150, taking written fraction cards and lighting which of the two numbers is the larger, with the test printed above it in the words it is written in rather than in a remembered name; a card whose two numbers are equal pours to exactly full and the tray prints, in words and with no figure standing beside it, that this one is improper and is one whole. Show the division writes the division under the tray, 420 by 150 at 660,610, with divisor, quotient and remainder each labelled, and draws a leader from the quotient to the filled circles and from the remainder to the parts still loose, so neither number stands on its own. Build it back runs the other way: a mixed number is placed on the tray, each whole one visibly breaks along its own ruled lines into the pinned number of parts, the broken parts slide into the loose ones and are counted in with them, and the single fraction is written out over the same lower number as before. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a count, a quotient or a remainder is asked for, with two extra keys that write the two places of a mixed number so the whole part and the fraction part are put down as two things rather than typed as one run of figures. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the parts a fraction counts are deep blue, the parts of that same whole which it leaves are amber, a whole shown entire or a bracket spanning one whole is green, a second writing of an amount already on the stage is rose, the greater of two fractions one of the chapter's rules can settle is vermilion, and a pair neither rule settles is sky blue, which is how this stage says undecided without saying wrong. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told from the rest by the drawn cut between them and by the label under it before it is ever told by a fill, and every cut, score line, cell edge and guide line is near-black. A fraction is drawn everywhere with its upper number above a level horizontal line and its lower number below, both upright and centred, and a mixed number is drawn as an upright whole number standing beside a stacked fraction. The pinned lower number is drawn in the same place, the same size and the same ink on every phase and in both directions of every conversion. It is the one handhold a child has while the other two numbers move, and a stage that let it drift would take that away at exactly the moment it is needed.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last tray the child filled, the whole ones and the loose parts still on it, and both readings written underneath with the lower number ringed in each.

phases.win: the improper cards fill at least one whole, and the one whose numbers match fills exactly with nothing over
phases.does: compares the two numbers of each fraction and pours the improper ones
phases.goal: an improper fraction is one whose upper number is not the smaller one
phases.says: Look at the two numbers. Is the one on top smaller, or is it not?
phases.check: Is 10/10 an improper fraction, and how much is it worth? Say which part of the test it passes on.
phases.feels: a card with two matching numbers fills its circle exactly and has nothing left over to stand beside it
phases.hands: Write 5/12, 12/5 and 7/7 on three cards and read each one out with the two numbers compared aloud: is the top one smaller than the bottom, or is it not? Then cut a paper circle into sevenths, hand over all seven pieces, and ask what they come to when they are put back together.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which of the two numbers on this card is written above the line? Second rung, the phase's: is that one smaller than the one below it, or is it not? Third rung: the tray is cut to a part size of four and the cards are poured one at a time so the test can be watched rather than recited. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: improper has been heard as top heavy, and a card whose two numbers match looks like neither one thing nor the other.
wrong.move: leaves 7/7 out of the improper cards, because it does not look like more than one whole.
wrong.screen: the test is printed above the sorter in the words it is written in, numerator greater than or equal to denominator, with greater and equal lit one after the other as two separate ways of passing it. The card is then poured: seven parts go into a circle ruled into seven, it fills right round, the heap is empty and nothing stands beside the full circle. The tray says in words that this one is improper and is one whole, and the child's sorting is left exactly as it was.

wrong.why: the test has been heard as being about which number is bigger, and twelve plainly is, so the card seems to pass.
wrong.move: calls 5/12 improper because twelve is the bigger of its two numbers.
wrong.screen: the sorter lights the two numbers in their places rather than by size, the upper one above the line and the lower one below it, and reads the test out with each one named as it is reached. The card is poured anyway: five parts go into a circle ruled into twelve and stop well short of filling it, with seven parts of that circle left amber and the green bracket spanning the whole drawn above them. The child's card stays where it was put.

phases.screen: the sorter holding several written fractions with the tray empty behind it
phases.soWhat: A fraction is improper when its upper number is greater than or equal to its lower number, which is a test on the two numbers and nothing else.
phases.concept: When the top is not the smaller one

phases.win: the mixed number is written with the whole part and the proper fraction in their places
phases.does: writes the whole count and the leftover parts into the two places of a mixed number
phases.goal: a mixed number is a whole number standing beside a proper fraction
phases.says: Count the full ones first. Now say what is left over beside them.
phases.check: Is 2 3/8 a mixed number or an improper fraction, and what is each of its parts counting?
phases.feels: two numbers written side by side, and each of them counts a different thing on the tray
phases.hands: Put two full paper plates of fifths on the table with three loose fifths beside them. Ask for the full plates to be counted first and the loose pieces second, and write the two counts in that order with a space between them. Then ask which of the two numbers would change if another loose piece arrived.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many whole ones are full on the tray? Second rung, the phase's: how many loose parts are lying beside them? Third rung: the tray is cut to one full whole and one loose part, so the two places can be filled from a picture with two things in it. Nothing already written is taken away.

wrong.why: the card is worth one whole, and one whole feels like something that ought to be written in the two places a mixed number has.
wrong.move: treats 8/8 as a mixed number and tries to write a whole one with a fraction part standing beside it.
wrong.screen: the card is poured and the circle fills right round, with the heap empty and the loose row beside the tray drawn and bare. The mixed number's second place is then read out for what it holds, a proper fraction, and there is no piece anywhere on the tray to put in it; the tray prints that a mixed number is a whole number with a proper fraction beside it and that this card has a whole number and nothing beside it. The single fraction reading stays up throughout and the child's writing is left standing.

wrong.why: both counts are true and both are standing on the tray, and nothing in a pair of numbers says which of the two places each belongs in.
wrong.move: writes the loose parts as the whole part and the full plates as the fraction part, swapping the two places over.
wrong.screen: the tray reads itself back with a leader drawn from each place of the mixed number to the thing it counts, the first place to the full circles and the second place to the loose pieces, and the part size pinned above is lit as the second place's lower number. The child's writing stays exactly as it was and the tray's reading is written underneath it, so two whole ones and three fifths and the swapped version stand one above the other and are poured out in turn.

phases.screen: two full wholes on the tray with some loose parts beside them
phases.soWhat: A mixed number is a whole number standing beside a proper fraction, which is a different kind of thing from a single fraction with one number above another.
phases.concept: A whole number with a part beside it

phases.win: the quotient points at the filled wholes, the remainder points at the loose parts, and the lower number has not moved
phases.does: pours, then fills in the quotient and the remainder from what the tray shows
phases.goal: dividing the upper number by the lower one gives the whole part and the remainder
phases.says: How many whole ones did you fill, and how many parts were left over?
phases.check: Write 29/8 as a mixed number, and tell me which part of the tray each of your numbers came from.
phases.feels: the division is the pouring written down, and each of its two answers is pointing at something on the tray
phases.hands: Hand over twenty-three loose sixths and a row of empty plates and let them be poured by hand. Then write the division out on paper, twenty-three divided by six, and draw an arrow from the quotient to the full plates and another from the remainder to the pieces still loose, before either number is copied into a mixed number.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many whole ones did the pouring fill? Second rung, the phase's: how many parts were still loose when it stopped? Third rung: the tray is cut to a heap of seven parts at a size of three, so the quotient and the remainder can both be counted by eye. Nothing already poured is tipped back.

wrong.why: the four printed steps name three numbers in quick succession and two of them belong to the fraction part, so the pair can be picked up the wrong way round without anything looking odd.
wrong.move: writes the remainder as the denominator and the divisor as the numerator, turning 23/6 into three whole ones and six fifths.
wrong.screen: the two leaders are drawn from the division to the tray and stay drawn: the quotient to the three full circles and the remainder to the five pieces still loose. The fraction part the child wrote is then built on the tray as it stands, six pieces where a whole one takes five, and it fills a circle and leaves one over, so a fraction part that is not a proper fraction is standing beside a whole number. The pinned part size is lit at the top throughout and the child's writing is left where it was.

wrong.why: the division was right, both numbers came out of it, and the conversion is plainly finished, so there seems to be nothing left to do.
wrong.move: converts correctly and leaves the fraction part as it comes out, writing fifty-two sixths as eight whole ones and four sixths.
wrong.screen: nothing is marked, because nothing here is wrong: the tray pours the heap and eight circles fill with four pieces over, exactly as the child wrote. The four loose pieces are then laid onto one more empty circle ruled into six, where they cover four of its parts, and the same four are laid onto a circle ruled into three, where they cover two of its parts exactly. Both writings are left standing side by side with a rose tie between them, because the second is a second writing of the first and not a correction of it.

phases.screen: a heap of loose parts with the division written empty under the tray
phases.soWhat: Divide the upper number by the lower one: the quotient is the whole part, the remainder is the new upper number, and the lower number stays exactly as it was.
phases.concept: Dividing to find the whole part

phases.win: the single fraction is written over the same lower number and the two readings agree
phases.does: breaks the whole ones into parts, adds the loose ones and writes the single fraction
phases.goal: a mixed number becomes one fraction by multiplying and adding
phases.says: Break every whole one into parts. Now count every part you are holding.
phases.check: Write 6 2/9 as a single fraction, and say where the nine in your answer came from.
phases.feels: every whole one breaks into exactly the number of pieces pinned at the top, and the counting does the rest
phases.hands: Give out four whole paper circles already ruled into sevenths and three loose sevenths. Break every circle along its own lines, push all the pieces into one heap and count them. Then write the count over the number of pieces one circle took, and compare that with multiplying the four by the seven and adding the three.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many pieces does one whole one break into? Second rung, the phase's: how many pieces do all your whole ones give between them? Third rung: the tray is cut to two whole ones at a part size of three, so the breaking and the counting can be done without the pad. Nothing broken is ever put back for the child.

wrong.why: the two numbers standing nearest each other are the four and the three, and adding them is the smallest move available.
wrong.move: adds the whole number to the upper number of the fraction part, writing 4 3/7 as seven sevenths.
wrong.screen: the seven over seven the child wrote is poured onto the tray and fills one circle exactly, with the heap empty and eleven of the twelve circles on the tray untouched. Beside it the four whole ones are broken along their own lines and counted into the heap, seven, fourteen, twenty-one, twenty-eight, and the three loose pieces are counted in after them to thirty-one. Both writings stay on the stage and neither is crossed through.

wrong.why: the two numbers written closest together on the page are the four and the three, and the lower number sits further away under its own line.
wrong.move: multiplies the whole number by the upper number of the fraction part instead of by the lower one, reaching fifteen sevenths.
wrong.screen: the breaking is run at walking pace with each circle counted out as it opens, and what comes out of one circle is the pinned number of parts rather than the numerator of anything; the pinned seven is lit at the top of the stage each time a circle breaks. The child's fifteen over seven is poured on a second tray and fills two circles with one over, while the real heap fills four with three over, and both trays are left standing.

phases.screen: a mixed number on the tray with the build it back control waiting
phases.soWhat: Multiply the whole number by the lower number, add the upper number of the fraction part, and write the total over that same lower number.

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the moment build it back is released on four whole ones and three loose sevenths. The whole circles do not vanish and reappear as a number. Each of them cracks along the ruled lines it has carried since it was drawn, seven pieces at a time, and the pieces fan out and slide across into the loose heap, where they are counted in one by one with the running count climbing seven, fourteen, twenty-one, twenty-eight. The three that were already loose join at the end, twenty-nine, thirty, thirty-one, and the single fraction writes itself as thirty-one over seven with the seven arriving from the pinned number at the top of the stage rather than from anywhere in the working. Press it again and every part flies home into a circle and closes up. Nothing else on the tray moves and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the sorter stands above an empty tray holding several written fraction cards face up, with the part size already pinned across the top of the stage and the heap untouched. On the second two whole circles on the tray are filled right round and a few loose parts lie beside them, with the two places of a mixed number ruled and empty underneath. On the third a heap of loose parts waits with the division drawn under the tray, its divisor printed and its quotient and remainder boxes open. On the fourth a mixed number stands on the tray already, its whole ones drawn whole and its loose parts beside them, with the build it back control lit. The running count at the top left holds the parts poured against the parts in the heap, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the top card of the sorter, or the loose parts beside the full circles, or the empty quotient box, or the nearest whole one waiting to be broken, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how many of these parts one whole one takes. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any heap of loose parts up to sixty at any part size up to twelve, with both readings, the sorter and the build it back control open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on testing a fraction for improper, on what a mixed number is made of, on dividing to find the whole part, and on writing a mixed number as one fraction.
voiceLines: Whole ones on the left, loose parts on the right, and every part the same size.
Look at the two numbers. Is the one on top smaller, or is it not?
Count the full ones first. Now say what is left over beside them.
How many whole ones did you fill, and how many parts were left over?
Break every whole one into parts. Now count every part you are holding.
A new heap. How many of these parts does one whole one take?
Free play. Any heap, any part size, both readings on and the build it back control open.
Pour it again slowly and watch both readings climb together underneath the tray.
Every heap counted both ways, and the number below the line never moved once.

observations.why: Seven parts of a whole cut into seven fill it exactly, so the card is worth one whole and no more.
observations.soWhat: Improper is a test on the two numbers, and equal numbers pass it, so 7/7 is improper and is exactly one.
observations.observe: A card whose two numbers were equal poured until the wholes were full and left nothing beside them.

observations.why: Dividing the count of parts by the size of a whole one is the pouring, written down.
observations.soWhat: The quotient is the whole part and the remainder is the new upper number, because that is what each of them counted.
observations.observe: The quotient always pointed at the filled circles and the remainder always pointed at the loose parts.

observations.why: Converting changes how the parts are counted and never cuts them into anything else.
observations.soWhat: The denominator stays the same whichever way you convert, so hold on to it while the other two numbers move.
observations.observe: The number below the line was the same before and after, in both directions, every time.

observations.why: The conversion was finished and correct; tidying the fraction part is a separate piece of work that follows it.
observations.soWhat: A mixed number is usually written with its fraction part reduced, and the two writings are the same amount.
observations.observe: One conversion left a fraction part that would still divide, and the tray accepted it.

phases.screen: the sorter holding several written fractions with the tray empty behind it
phases.win: the improper cards fill at least one whole, and the one whose numbers match fills exactly with nothing over
phases.traceback: Each card rings its larger number (both when they are equal), pours into circles cut to its own bottom number, and is tagged improper or proper; the child's sorting stays where it was put.
ladder: On each card, which number is written above the line?
Check every card, one at a time, top number first.
Ten on top and ten below. Is the top one smaller?
Is that one smaller than the one below it, or is it not?
Take one card at a time. Point to the top number, then to the bottom one.

phases.screen: two full wholes on the tray with some loose parts beside them
phases.win: the mixed number is written with the whole part and the proper fraction in their places
phases.traceback: A leader runs from the whole number to the full circles and another from the fraction to the loose parts, each place labelled, and the two together are bracketed as a mixed number.
ladder: Which number counts the full circles, and which counts the loose parts?
How many whole ones are full on the tray?
Is a whole number standing beside the fraction here?
How many loose parts are lying beside them?
Point to the full circles, then to the loose parts. Each one has its own place in the number.

phases.screen: a heap of loose parts with the division written empty under the tray
phases.win: the quotient points at the filled wholes, the remainder points at the loose parts, and the lower number has not moved
phases.traceback: The heap pours one whole at a time with the quotient counting up, the parts left loose are ringed as the remainder, and the mixed number writes itself beside the single fraction.
ladder: Count the circles that filled right round.
After the last full pour, is anything left in the heap?
How many eighths are left when no more wholes will fill?
How many parts were still loose when it stopped?
Count the pours: each one is a whole. Parts too few to fill a whole stay loose.

phases.screen: a mixed number on the tray with the build it back control waiting
phases.win: the single fraction is written over the same lower number and the two readings agree
phases.traceback: Every whole one breaks at walking pace and is counted on by the part size, the loose parts are counted in after them, and the single fraction writes itself over the same bottom number.
ladder: How many pieces does one whole one break into?
Six wholes make how many ninths altogether?
Count the sixths from the broken wholes first, then add the loose ones.
How many pieces do all your whole ones give between them?

items.winSay: Seven sevenths fills one circle exactly, with nothing over.
Nothing is left over, so 45/9 is a whole number.
Four sixths cover two thirds, so it is also 5 2/3, or 17/3.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: Each card rings its larger number (both when they are equal), pours into circles cut to its own bottom number, and is tagged improper or proper; the child's sorting stays where it was put.
Phase 2: A leader runs from the whole number to the full circles and another from the fraction to the loose parts, each place labelled, and the two together are bracketed as a mixed number.
Phase 3: The heap pours one whole at a time with the quotient counting up, the parts left loose are ringed as the remainder, and the mixed number writes itself beside the single fraction.
Phase 4: Every whole one breaks at walking pace and is counted on by the part size, the loose parts are counted in after them, and the single fraction writes itself over the same bottom number.

voice.opening: A tray of whole ones, and fractions to pour into it.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: Every heap counted both ways, and the number below the line never moved once.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

items.planQuestion: Of 5/12, 12/5 and 7/7, say which are improper fractions and which one of them is exactly one whole.

question.en: Of 5/12, 12/5 and 7/7, drag the improper fractions down to the tray. Then press enter.

items.planAnswer: 12/5 and 7/7 are improper, and 7/7 is exactly one whole

items.planQuestion: Which of 11/6, 4/13 and 5/5 are improper fractions?

question.en: Now 11/6, 4/13 and 5/5. Which of these are improper?

items.planQuestion: Is 10/10 an improper fraction, and how much is it worth?

question.en: Is 10/10 an improper fraction, and how much is it worth?

items.planAnswer: Yes, it is improper, and it is worth exactly one whole

items.planQuestion: Write a mixed number made of three whole ones and two fifths, and say which part of it is the proper fraction.

question.en: Read the tray and write the mixed number it holds.

items.planQuestion: Is 3 2/5 an improper fraction or a mixed number, and what is it made of?

question.en: Is 3 2/5 an improper fraction or a mixed number? Look at what it is made of.

items.planAnswer: A mixed number, made of the whole number 3 standing beside the proper fraction 2/5

items.planQuestion: Is 2 3/8 a mixed number or an improper fraction?

question.en: And 2 3/8? Is it a mixed number or an improper fraction?

items.planAnswer: A mixed number, because it is a whole number standing beside a proper fraction

ask.en: Write it as a mixed number

question.en: Now pour 45/9 and write what it makes.

items.planAnswer: 5, because nine goes into forty-five five times with nothing left over

question.en: Last one: 29/8. Pour it the same way and write it.
Now 6 2/9. Break it back and write it as one fraction.

items.planQuestion: Write 5 4/6 as a single fraction, then say what the same amount looks like once the fraction part is reduced.

question.en: Last, 5 4/6. What single fraction is it?

items.planAnswer: 34/6, and once reduced it is 5 2/3, which is 17/3
